conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea for about five days now. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it started after I ate at a diner. I felt off that night, and then the next day I couldn’t keep anything down. No fever or belly pain, just constant nausea and loose stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your kidney function came back a bit high—creatinine of 2.7, which is above your baseline. That suggests some dehydration. We’ll start you on IV fluids right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I did stop my Bumex when my doctor told me, but I just haven’t been able to drink much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll help you rehydrate. Given your history—liver transplant, chronic diarrhea, and cervical spine hardware—we need to be careful. We’re going to run some tests to see what’s causing this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine culture came back positive for Group B Streptococcus. It’s not common, but we’ll treat it with antibiotics since you’re immunocompromised.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I didn’t have any burning or urgency this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. You’ve had UTIs before, and even without symptoms, we treat them to prevent complications. You’ll get a 7-day course of cefpodoxime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve taken that before. It usually helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an abdominal X-ray yesterday. It showed a nonspecific bowel pattern—no obstruction. But you’re still vomiting, so we’re scheduling a CT scan today to look deeper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could this be related to my neck hardware? I’ve had trouble swallowing before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good point. Your history of cervical fusion raises concern. The CT will help us see if there’s any erosion into the esophagus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT of your head was normal—no stroke or bleed. But we’re still worried about your swallowing. We’re going to do a gastrograffin swallow study tomorrow to check for leaks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. It’s uncomfortable, but I’ll do it if it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The swallowing study showed no leak, which is good. But the esophagus is very close to your cervical hardware. We’re concerned there might be erosion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that could be why I’m nauseous? Because something’s pressing on my throat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re scheduling an EGD today to look directly. But we’ll stop if we see any sign of hardware exposure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did the EGD. We saw what looks like a fistula—your esophagus may be eroding into the cervical hardware. We stopped the procedure to avoid injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Can they fix that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: ENT, neurosurgery, and transplant surgery are all involved. Right now, surgery is too risky because of your malnutrition and the immunosuppressant you’re on—sirolimus—it impairs healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll stop sirolimus and switch you to mycophenolate and prednisone. That should help your body heal. But for now, you can’t eat by mouth safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait—you mean I can’t eat at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. We’re going to place a feeding tube directly into your stomach and intestine—a GJ tube—so you can get nutrition without using your esophagus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds intense. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s done under CT guidance. A specialist will place it. You’ll be sedated. It’s the safest way to feed you until we can consider surgery later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart rate has been slow—down to the 30s at night. Your ECG shows a prolonged QT interval. You were on ondansetron for nausea. That can worsen QT prolongation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had heart issues before. I was told not to take ciprofloxacin because of that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. So we’ve stopped ondansetron and reduced your narcotics. Your heart rate is improving. You must avoid any medications that prolong QT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No Zofran, no cipro. I’ll remember.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been complaining of left lower quadrant pain. The CT showed no diverticulitis, but there’s a lot of stool in your rectum. It’s likely impaction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I haven’t had a good bowel movement in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you a Dulcolax suppository. You passed a large amount this morning. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Feels like a weight’s been lifted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep you on stool softeners to prevent it from happening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to place a PICC line today so we can give you IV nutrition—TPN—until the GJ tube is ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another line? I already have so many tubes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s a lot. But TPN is temporary. Once the GJ tube is in, we’ll stop the PICC. It’s just to support you during this transition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC is in place. We’ve started TPN. You’ll get all your calories and nutrients through this line for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I need that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Until the GJ tube is placed and working. That’s scheduled for day after tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show you’re severely malnourished—low BMI, low albumin, temporal wasting. That’s why healing is so hard. The GJ tube will help reverse that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve always struggled to eat enough. Even before this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and with chronic diarrhea and your transplant, it’s been a long battle. But with high-calorie tube feeds, we can rebuild your strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—the GJ tube was placed successfully under CT guidance. It goes straight into your stomach and then into the jejunum. You can start tube feeds tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll never eat normally again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. If you heal and gain weight, surgery might be an option later. For now, the tube keeps you safe and nourished.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started tube feeds at a low rate. We’ll increase slowly. You’re on a high-calorie formula called TwoCal HF.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel nauseous sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common at first. We’ve added low-dose lorazepam for breakthrough nausea. Avoids QT issues. Let us know if it’s not helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is down to 1.3—your kidneys are recovering. And your weight is up by two pounds. The tube feeds are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a little stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’re also switching your diarrhea med back to opium tincture. C. diff tests were negative, so it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat urine culture is negative. You’ve completed your antibiotics. No signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want another UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning your discharge. You’ll go home with the GJ tube, on tube feeds 24/7. You’ll follow up with ENT, neurosurgery, and transplant clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be on mycophenolate and prednisone instead of sirolimus. Keep taking your pain meds, opium tincture, and lorazepam for nausea. No ondansetron.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: your heart rate is stable, labs are improving, and you’re tolerating feeds. You’re cleared for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about managing the tube at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A nurse will train you and your caregiver. You’ll have supplies and a 24-hour hotline. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Remember: follow up in one week, call if nausea worsens, and avoid QT-prolonging drugs. You’ve made great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.
